newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cement makers to meet or surpass forecasts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cement makers to meet or surpass forecasts.

text.p: U.S. cement companies are set to meet or surpass Wall Street's quarterly earnings forecasts as construction rumbles throughout the United States, pushing cement prices to their highest level in years, industry analysts say.
"I'm very bullish on cement," said Jack Kasprzak at Scott & Stringfellow.

The three largest U.S.-owned companies have been working at capacity to meet demand from office builders and road repair crews and selling cement at some of the highest prices in at least three years, analysts say.
John Stanley of Dillon, Read & Co said the prices -- as well as high productivity at their plants -- were generating huge cash flows for Southdown Inc, Medusa Corp and Lone Star Industries Inc.
"Just holding around current price levels will generate an embarrassment of financial riches for the industry," he said in a recent report on the sector.
Southdown Chief Financial Officer James Persky told Reuters the net selling price of its cement had risen to $64.19 a (short) ton this year from $60.69 in 1995.
The price compares to a national average of about $65 a (short) ton, according to calculations made by Stanley.
Southdown of Houston, Texas is the third largest producer in the United States with an annual capacity of 6.5 million (short) tons.
Holman of Swiss Holderbank Financiere Glarus AG and Lafarge Corp of France's Lafarge SA are the largest.

John Bermudez of Merrill Lynch said California's economic recovery had allowed Southdown to raise its price by $8 a (short) ton in the state and come to par with what other companies were charging in other parts of the country.
"They have a lot of exposure in the southern California market, where there's been good turnaround (in construction)," he said, adding that other companies had risen prices by up to $2 since April.

On July 1, the U.S. Commerce Department reported total construction spending at an annualized and seasonally adjusted $585.0 billion for May, slightly higher than the $562.3 billion for the same month last year.

"Construction in general is steady ... There's no boom, but it has continued unabated," said Kasprzak at Scott and Stringfellow. "There's no speculation, so there are few risks of a precipitous decline in the next year or two."
Kasprzak said he saw U.S. cement consumption rising higher than the 100 million (short) tons consumed last year.

Merrill Lynch's Bermudez said Lone Star of Stamford, Connecticut was benefiting from construction in another part of the country. "The northeast has picked up quite measurably, especially commercial building," he said.
Stanley said the huge cash flows had enabled the companies to modernize their plants, pay off debt and repurchase stock.
In his report, he listed Medusa of Cleveland Heights, Ohio had one of the most liquid balance sheets.
"Medusa should remain a highly profitable company with the potential for mid-teens EPS (earnings per share) growth depending on how well it deploys its rich cash flow," he said.

Although they are the largest U.S.-owned cement companies, they only control about a third of production. The rest is held by foreign-owned companies like Holderbank and Lafarge. FIRST CALL ESTIMATES VS REPORTED YEAR AGO COMPANY (IN DOLLARS) Q2 YEAR AGO RESULTS DATE
